question: Can positive homogeneity turn ordinary squared-weight decay into an equivalent nonsmooth group penalty whose proximal operator reaches balanced, structurally sparse neural-network solutions faster than SGD with weight decay?

key_findings.claim: At a minimum-squared-norm representation, every positively homogeneous unit is balanced: its incoming and outgoing weight norms are equal.
key_findings.evidence: Scaling a unit's incoming weights by alpha and outgoing weights by alpha inverse preserves its function. Minimizing the sum of their squared norms over that orbit gives equal norms, so any unbalanced representation can be rescaled to reduce weight decay without changing the loss.

key_findings.claim: The paper establishes equivalence of global solution functions, up to balancing rescalings, between squared weight decay and a disjoint-layer sum of incoming/outgoing norm products.
key_findings.evidence: For alternating homogeneous-unit couplings, every parameter appears once; at a balanced global minimum, half the paired squared norm equals the product of the two norms. Theorem 4.1 therefore maps global minimizers between F-lambda and G-lambda after any needed rescaling. This is a global-minimizer equivalence, not an equality of objectives or optimization trajectories away from balance.

key_findings.claim: PathProx converts the norm-product form into group soft-thresholding by fixing each selected incoming vector to unit norm and adds an explicit across-layer balance operation.
key_findings.evidence: Each iteration takes a loss-gradient step, projects selected incoming vectors to the unit sphere, applies the group-lasso proximal map to outgoing vectors, and equalizes total path norm across paired layers. Exact zeros therefore remove whole neurons or convolutional channels rather than individual weights.

key_findings.claim: The stated convergence transfer from the constrained path objective to a stationary point of the original weight-decay objective is not established by the appendix.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 4.3 says a limit point is stationary for both objectives after rescaling. Appendix C verifies a cited stochastic-proximal theorem only for the unit-sphere constrained group penalty, under an imposed compact output-weight set and diminishing steps. It never proves that a stationary point of that problem maps to a stationary point of squared weight decay; global-minimizer equivalence from Theorem 4.1 is insufficient for that local claim.

anchors.section: Appendix C, constrained problem and Theorem C.1

key_findings.claim: The faster-convergence evidence is iteration-based and does not establish lower training time or scalability.
key_findings.evidence: On one 1,000-example factorized MNIST MLP, Figure 4 compares best-learning-rate curves at fixed lambda and shows PathProx reducing the weight-decay objective faster per iteration. No wall-clock, FLOP, memory, throughput, optimizer-state, or accelerator analysis accounts for projections, group thresholding, layer balancing, and factorization, and the larger VGG experiments do not report convergence curves.

anchors.section: 5.1 PathProx Minimizes Weight Decay Objective Faster

key_findings.claim: Generalization improvements are small and mixed, and most comparisons do not hold the regularized objective fixed.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 has PathProx slightly worse on clean full MNIST and corrupted CIFAR-10, while improving several other cells. Appendix Table 5 shows independently validation-selected lambdas differing by 10x on both MNIST tasks and by 3x on SVHN, so those rows compare tuned procedures rather than two optimizers minimizing the same F-lambda. Only four post-selection runs are used for standard errors.

key_findings.claim: PathProx can induce substantial structured sparsity, but the effect is architecture- and setting-dependent and is not a compression benchmark.
key_findings.evidence: The reported active-unit fraction falls to about 48 percent on CIFAR-10 VGG19 and 44 percent on SVHN VGG19, but remains 98.3 to 99.95 percent on two MNIST settings. The dedicated MNIST MLP curve shows better accuracy at high sparsity than SGD with weight decay, lasso, or group lasso after additional pruning and retraining, without parameter/FLOP speedup, dense accuracy matching, modern pruning baselines, or deployment latency.

anchors.section: Table 1 and 5.3 PathProx Finds Sparse Solutions Faster

method.core_idea: Exploit ReLU rescaling symmetry to replace paired squared weights with an equivalent norm-product penalty at global optima, then optimize a unit-normalized group-lasso reparameterization with proximal thresholding.
method.mechanism: Alternating pairs of linear or convolutional layers define non-overlapping homogeneous units. Incoming weights are gradient-updated and normalized; outgoing weights are gradient-updated and shrunk by max(0, 1-lambda-times-step/norm); zero groups deactivate a unit. A rescaling step equalizes total paired-layer path norms, while unpaired final weights retain standard weight decay.
assumptions: Relevant activations and pooling operations are positively one-homogeneous and their biases are scaled consistently.
Global solutions exist and function-preserving rescaling can reach balanced representatives.
For convergence, data and iterates lie in bounded definable sets and step sizes are non-summable but square-summable.
Treating only disjoint alternating homogeneous units is an adequate practical surrogate for symmetric treatment of every hidden unit.
Iteration count is an informative proxy for training efficiency despite additional proximal and balancing work.

techniques.role: Uses positive-homogeneous scale symmetry to characterize minimum-squared-norm representations.
Replaces paired sums of squared weights with products of incoming and outgoing group norms.
Fixes incoming group norms so the norm product becomes a separable outgoing group-lasso penalty.
Shrinks or exactly zeros whole neuron/channel output groups after the loss-gradient step.
Rescales layers without changing the network function so total path norm is equal across layer couplings.
Introduces extra linear factors to define homogeneous units for every target group in selected experiments.

evaluations.setting: 1,000-example MNIST subset with factorized three-layer 400-unit MLP
evaluations.result: At lambda 1e-4 and each method's best learning rate, PathProx reduces the objective faster than SGD on either the path or squared-weight objective.
evaluations.baseline: SGD with path penalty and SGD with weight decay; no wall-clock or adaptive-optimizer baseline.

evaluations.setting: Full MNIST with six-layer MLP and subset MNIST with factorized MLP
evaluations.metric: Clean and MNIST-C accuracy plus active-unit fraction
evaluations.result: Changes are within roughly 0.1 to 1.7 percentage points; PathProx leaves 98.3 to 99.95 percent of selected units active.
evaluations.baseline: Validation-tuned SGD weight decay with different selected lambda on both tasks.

evaluations.result: CIFAR clean improves from 90.41 to 90.79 while corruption accuracy changes from 60.78 to 60.71; SVHN clean improves from 94.68 to 95.51. PathProx retains about 48.29 and 44.02 percent of channels, respectively.
evaluations.baseline: Validation-tuned SGD weight decay; no ResNet, ImageNet, modern optimizer, pruning, or latency baseline.

evaluations.setting: MNIST three-layer 800-unit MLP sparsity sweep with 10,000-step post-pruning retraining
evaluations.metric: Test accuracy as a function of retained active units
evaluations.result: PathProx reaches sparser solutions than weight decay and outperforms naive SGD with lasso or group lasso at matched reported sparsity.
evaluations.baseline: Weight decay, lasso, and group lasso trained by SGD; no proximal lasso/group-lasso or contemporary structured-pruning baseline.

evaluations.result: Weight normalization alone slightly lowers weight-decay accuracy; removing layer balancing from PathProx reduces accuracy from 90.79 to 90.58 while retaining even fewer channels.
evaluations.baseline: Weight decay with projection and PathProx without layer balancing.

limitations: Author-stated: alternating disjoint layer groups treat homogeneous units asymmetrically; a formulation handling all units uniformly is future work.
Author-stated: convergence imports bounded-iterate and diminishing-step assumptions from a general theorem rather than deriving realistic constant-step behavior.
Reviewer inference: the stationary-point correspondence to the original weight-decay objective is asserted but not proved in Appendix C.
Reviewer inference: comparisons tune lambda separately, so most accuracy results do not test optimizer quality on an identical objective.
Reviewer inference: four post-selection runs after a one-seed grid search give weak uncertainty and do not include paired-seed or multiple-comparison analysis.
Reviewer inference: only small vision datasets, MLPs, and VGG19 are tested; no transformers, normalization-heavy modern networks, large-scale data, or AdamW setting is covered.
Reviewer inference: speed claims use iterations rather than time or compute, and sparsity claims omit realized FLOP, memory, and latency reductions.
failure_modes: Non-homogeneous activations, normalization layers, residual branches, or unscaled biases can invalidate the rescaling equivalence or make grouping ambiguous.
Projection to a unit sphere is singular at zero and changes the optimizer geometry sharply when a group is pruned or reintroduced.
Exact group thresholding can irreversibly remove useful capacity early under noisy minibatch gradients or an aggressive lambda-step product.
Layer balancing can amplify one layer while shrinking another and interact poorly with adaptive preconditioners, momentum, or finite precision.
A sparse parameterization can have no practical acceleration when kernels remain dense or channel shapes are not physically compacted.
Equivalent global solution functions do not imply that the two nonconvex algorithms visit corresponding local minima or stationary points.
reusable_insights: Exploit model symmetries to expose nonsmooth structure that is hidden inside a smooth-looking parameter penalty.
State explicitly whether equivalence concerns functions, balanced parameter representatives, global minima, stationary points, or full optimization trajectories.
Compare optimizers at the same regularization coefficient and report both per-iteration and per-compute convergence.
Translate exact group zeros into measured parameter, FLOP, memory, and wall-clock gains after physical compaction.
Ablate normalization, thresholding, and layer balancing separately under matched updates to identify the source of gains.
open_questions: Can one derive and compute a symmetric proximal operator that treats every overlapping homogeneous unit rather than alternating layer pairs?
Under what conditions do stationary points, not only global minimizers, correspond between squared weight decay and the norm-product objective?
Does PathProx remain stable and advantageous with residual networks, batch/layer normalization, attention, and AdamW-scale training?
How do pruning irreversibility, minibatch noise, lambda schedules, and proximal momentum affect support identification?
Do exact group zeros improve certified or adversarial robustness after controlling for clean accuracy and compute?

competitive_landscape.title: Efficient Proximal Mapping of the 1-path-norm of Shallow Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Latorre et al. derive and benchmark proximal maps for an explicit 1-path norm in shallow networks; PathProx instead uses an l2 norm-product that is globally equivalent to ordinary squared weight decay and extends the grouping to deep MLPs and CNNs.

competitive_landscape.title: A General Family of Stochastic Proximal Gradient Methods for Deep Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: ProxGen supports broad nonsmooth and nonconvex regularizers with adaptive positive preconditioners; PathProx contributes a problem-specific reparameterization and closed-form group threshold tied to weight-decay symmetry.

competitive_landscape.title: Feature Learning in L2-regularized DNNs: Attraction/Repulsion and Sparsity
competitive_landscape.difference: Jacot et al. reformulate l2-regularized deep networks through hidden representations and prove width bounds for local minima; PathProx focuses on a balanced parameter-orbit reformulation and an algorithm intended to reach sparse representatives quickly.

competitive_landscape.title: spred: Solving L1 Penalty with SGD
competitive_landscape.difference: spred gives an exact differentiable reparameterization for generic l1-regularized objectives so ordinary SGD can obtain sparsity; PathProx derives group sparsity from the homogeneous network's existing weight-decay equivalence and uses an explicit proximal step.

competitive_landscape.title: 1-Path-Norm Regularization of Deep Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Latorre et al. approximate the intractable deep 1-path-norm proximal map for general architectures and test noisy-label robustness; PathProx's simpler l2 group map depends on alternating homogeneous units but preserves the global solutions of standard weight decay.

competitive_landscape.title: Rotational Equilibrium: How Weight Decay Balances Learning Across Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Kosson et al. analyze how weight decay sets neuron norms and effective learning rates during ordinary training, including equilibrium dynamics; PathProx enforces unit and layer balance explicitly to expose a proximal sparse penalty.

competitive_landscape.title: Win: Weight-Decay-Integrated Nesterov Acceleration for Faster Network Training
competitive_landscape.difference: Win integrates a dynamic weight-decay-inspired regularizer into Nesterov-style adaptive optimization and provides broad acceleration analysis; PathProx targets exact structured zeros through homogeneity and group thresholding but lacks large-scale adaptive-optimizer experiments.

novelty_assessment: Author claim: this is the first practical use of the equivalent l2 norm-product form of homogeneous-network weight decay, yielding a proximal algorithm that converges faster and finds sparse, robust solutions. Reviewer inference after primary-source comparison: the balanced-orbit connection was known, and proximal path-norm and general neural proximal optimizers already existed, but tying a simple group soft-threshold specifically to the global solution set of standard weight decay is a clear, useful algorithmic synthesis. The evidence supports faster objective reduction per iteration on a small matched task and sometimes dramatic structured sparsity. It does not yet establish faster wall-clock training, uniformly better generalization, modern-scale usefulness, or the claimed stationary-point transfer back to the original objective.
reviewer_notes: Read all twenty-four extracted pages, including every theorem and proof, the exact alternating-layer algorithm, convergence assumptions, all task tables, hyperparameter grids, run-count protocol, component ablations, and references. I separated global balanced-representative equivalence from the unproved stationary-point correspondence, audited every Table 1 direction and Table 5 lambda mismatch, and checked seven primary-source proximal, path-norm, weight-decay, sparsity, and acceleration competitors through August 2026.
